qs.q: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification, which specific astrocytoma is categorized as Grade IV?
qs.e: Glioblastoma is classified by the WHO as a Grade IV astrocytoma and represents the majority of high-grade astrocytomas. Pilocytic astrocytomas are Grade I, diffuse astrocytomas are Grade II, and anaplastic astrocytomas are Grade III.

qs.q: What is the approximate proportion of pediatric brain tumors represented by the group including juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma, diffuse astrocytomas, ependymoma, and craniopharyngioma?
qs.e: Eighty percent (80%) of pediatric tumors consist of juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma/PNET, diffuse astrocytomas, ependymoma, and craniopharyngioma. This group forms the vast majority of childhood CNS presentations.

qs.q: Which genetic condition is specifically linked to subependymal giant cell astrocytomas?
qs.e: Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC) is associated with subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. NF-2 is linked to schwannomas via gene deletion on chromosome 22.

qs.q: A 48-year-old man with a brain anaplastic astrocytoma later develops splenic/renal pain, hematuria, and massive bilateral pulmonary emboli. Most likely cardiovascular lesion?
o: Tear in the ascending aortic intima
qs.e: High-grade glioma + arterial and venous thromboembolic events = Trousseau syndrome (paraneoplastic hypercoagulability). Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis produces sterile mitral vegetations that embolize systemically.
